description: Emma arrives in the small town of Blackwood just before Halloween after receiving a mysterious letter from her grandmother. She is told to stay at an old house on Willow Road, but strange events soon make her wonder why her grandmother sent her there.

chapters.title: The Last October Night
chapters.content:
The train arrived in Blackwood just before sunset.

Emma rested her forehead against the cold window and watched the last light of October disappear behind the trees. The landscape had been changing for the past hour. The wide fields and small towns that had accompanied her journey were gone, replaced by dense forests whose dark branches seemed to stretch endlessly into the gray sky. A thin layer of fog covered the ground, drifting between the trees and occasionally rising high enough to hide the distant hills.

She checked her phone again. There was still no signal.

October 28.

She looked at the date for a moment before putting the phone away. It was only three days before Halloween, and yet the thought of the holiday had nothing to do with the reason she was traveling to Blackwood. She had never been there before, and until three days ago, she had barely known the town existed.

The letter in her coat pocket was the reason she had come.

Emma had read it so many times that she could almost remember every word without looking.

Her grandmother had written it in her usual careful handwriting, but something about the message had been different from her other letters. There had been no small talk, no questions about Emma's work or friends, no mention of the weather or the neighbors. Only a few sentences.

Emma,

If you are reading this, I need you to go to Blackwood.

Stay at the old house on Willow Road.

Do not leave before Halloween.

There are things about our family that you need to know.

Please trust me.

Her grandmother had signed her name beneath the last sentence.

Margaret.

Three days earlier, Emma had received the letter in the morning. That same afternoon, Margaret had been taken to the hospital after suddenly becoming ill. Emma had tried calling her several times, but there had been no answer. When she finally called the hospital, a nurse told her that her grandmother was resting and could not receive visitors.

Emma had wanted to go to the hospital immediately, but Margaret had always hated being treated as if she were fragile. More importantly, the letter had made one thing clear: she wanted Emma in Blackwood.

So Emma had packed a suitcase, canceled her plans for the week, and taken the first train she could find.

She still wasn't sure why she had obeyed.

Perhaps it was because her grandmother had never asked her for anything like this before. Perhaps it was because Margaret had always been a difficult woman to understand, and Emma had spent most of her life wondering what she wasn't being told. Or perhaps it was simply because, despite everything, she trusted her.

The train began to slow.

Emma looked through the window again and saw a small sign beside the tracks.

BLACKWOOD — NEXT STOP

She sat up.

The carriage was almost empty. An elderly man slept near the door with his head tilted against the window, while a young couple whispered to each other several seats away. At the opposite end of the carriage, a woman wearing a long dark coat sat alone.

Emma had noticed her earlier.

Now she realized the woman was looking directly at her.

Their eyes met.

The woman immediately turned toward the window.

Emma frowned, wondering if she had imagined it. She glanced at the woman again, but this time the stranger didn't move.

The train entered a tunnel.

Darkness filled the windows, and the reflection of the passengers appeared in the glass. Emma could see her own face staring back at her, pale beneath the carriage lights. Then the lights flickered.

Once.

Twice.

The entire carriage went dark.

Someone gasped.

The train continued through the tunnel, its wheels producing a deep metallic rhythm beneath the floor. Emma could hear the couple whispering nervously and the old man waking with a confused sound.

Then, very close behind her, a voice whispered:

— Don't go to the house.

Emma turned around.

There was no one there.

The lights came back on.

The old man was still sitting in his seat. The young couple were looking at each other. The woman in the dark coat was no longer by the window.

Emma looked toward the carriage door.

It was closed.

She stood up and walked toward it, but before she could reach it, the train emerged from the tunnel.

Blackwood appeared outside.

The town was smaller than Emma had imagined. A few rows of houses stretched along narrow streets, their roofs and chimneys barely visible through the evening mist. Almost every building seemed to have some kind of Halloween decoration: pumpkins sat on doorsteps, orange lights hung from windows, and paper bats were attached to shop signs.

For a brief moment, Emma smiled.

It looked peaceful.

Then she noticed how empty the streets were.

The train stopped with a long metallic screech.

Emma took her suitcase and stepped onto the platform. Cold air immediately touched her face. She looked around, expecting to see people waiting for the train, but there was almost no one there. An old station building stood beside the tracks, its windows dark and dusty. A wooden bench sat beneath a lamp, and above it hung a large clock.

Emma checked her phone.

6:18 p.m.

She looked at the station clock.

6:30.

She frowned and checked her phone again.

The difference was twelve minutes.

Maybe the clock was broken.

Emma was about to walk toward the station entrance when a railway employee passed her carrying a small suitcase.

— Excuse me. Do you know where I can find Willow Road?

The man stopped.

For a moment, he didn't answer.

His eyes moved from Emma to her suitcase and then back to her face.

— Willow Road?

— Yes.

— Are you staying there?

Emma nodded.

— My grandmother owns a house there.

The man's expression changed.

— What's her name?

— Margaret Carter.

The man became completely still.

— Margaret?

— Do you know her?

He looked toward the dark railway tracks.

— I knew her a long time ago.

Emma waited, but he said nothing more.

— Could you tell me how to get there?

The man finally pointed toward the town.

— Follow the main road until you reach the church. Turn left after the church. Willow Road is about fifteen minutes from there.

— Thank you.

Emma turned to leave, but something about his expression made her stop.

— Is there something wrong with the house?

The man didn't answer immediately. When he finally looked at her again, his face had become strangely serious.

— It's been empty for a long time.

— My grandmother still owns it.

— I know.

He walked into the station before Emma could ask how he knew.

She stood on the platform for another moment, unsettled by the exchange. Then she picked up her suitcase and started toward town.

The streets were quieter than they had appeared from the train. Most of the shops were still open, and Halloween decorations covered their windows, but there were few people outside. A bakery displayed cakes shaped like pumpkins, a bookstore had a sign advertising Halloween stories, and a small café had painted ghosts around its door.

Emma passed a row of houses decorated with carved pumpkins and strings of orange lights. Somewhere in the distance, a dog barked. The sound was quickly swallowed by the fog.

She checked her phone again.

Still no signal.

As she reached the end of the main street, she heard a church bell.

Once.

Emma stopped.

The sound echoed through the town.

Twice.

She looked toward the church tower, but the fog made it difficult to see.

Three times.

The bell stopped.

Emma waited.

Nothing else happened.

She continued walking.

A few minutes later, she reached an intersection. A wooden sign pointed in three directions.

CHURCH — 5 MINUTES

MARKET SQUARE — 3 MINUTES

WILLOW ROAD — 15 MINUTES

Emma stared at the last sign.

She thought about the letter in her pocket.

Stay at the old house on Willow Road.

She had expected the trip to feel strange. She hadn't expected the town itself to feel as though it were waiting for something.

Emma turned toward Willow Road.

The fog thickened almost immediately.

Behind her, the lights of the town became blurred and distant. Ahead, the road disappeared between tall trees.

She tightened her grip on the suitcase and continued walking.

She didn't notice the old woman standing across the street, watching her from beneath the awning of a closed shop.

The woman remained there until Emma disappeared into the fog.

Only then did she look toward the railway station.

The old clock still showed 6:30.

The woman whispered something under her breath.

— She came back.

Far beyond the town, somewhere among the trees, a church bell began to ring again.

Once.

Twice.

Three times.

Emma stopped walking.

She turned toward the sound.

The fog had already swallowed the road behind her.

chapters.title: Welcome to Blackwood
chapters.content:
Emma remained still for several seconds, listening to the last echo of the church bell disappear into the fog. The road ahead was barely visible, a narrow strip of wet pavement winding between tall trees whose branches met overhead. She could no longer see the lights of the town behind her, and for the first time since leaving the train station, she felt completely alone.

She reached into her coat pocket and touched the letter.

Stay at the old house on Willow Road.

The words suddenly seemed less like a request and more like a warning.

Emma shook the thought away. She had spent the entire journey imagining things, and now the unfamiliar town, the darkness, and the fog were making everything feel more mysterious than it really was. There had to be a simple explanation for the strange clock, the silent railway employee, and the bell.

She started walking again.

The houses became more frequent as the road curved around a small hill. Most were old, with wooden fences and narrow gardens, but several had been decorated for Halloween. Pumpkins sat on doorsteps, paper ghosts hung from trees, and strings of orange lights glowed softly through the mist.

The decorations should have made the town feel cheerful.

Instead, Emma found herself wondering why almost every house had its curtains closed.

She reached a small market square and stopped.

The square was surrounded by old buildings, their upper floors rising several stories above the narrow shops. In the center stood a stone fountain covered in moss. Children in costumes ran around it while their parents watched from the sidewalks. A group of teenagers carried bags of candy toward a bakery, laughing as they tried to scare one another.

The ordinary scene made Emma relax.

Perhaps she had been worrying for nothing.

She pulled her suitcase toward a small café on the corner. A brass bell rang above the door when she entered.

— Good evening!

The woman behind the counter smiled.

She looked to be in her sixties, with gray hair tied loosely behind her head and a green sweater decorated with tiny orange pumpkins.

— Good evening. I'm sorry to bother you, but could I ask you something?

— Of course. You look like you've just arrived.

Emma smiled.

— I did. I'm looking for Willow Road.

The woman's expression changed so subtly that Emma almost missed it.

— Willow Road?

— Yes.

— Why are you looking for it?

Emma hesitated.

— My grandmother owns a house there.

The woman put down the cup she was holding.

— What's your grandmother's name?

— Margaret Carter.

The woman's face went pale.

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

— Margaret? — she finally asked.

— Yes. Do you know her?

The woman looked toward the window before answering.

— I knew her a long time ago.

Emma pulled a chair away from a nearby table.

— Then maybe you can help me. She sent me here, but she didn't give me very many details.

The woman remained behind the counter.

— What kind of details?

— She told me to stay at the house until Halloween. That's all.

The woman stared at her.

— You shouldn't stay there.

Emma frowned.

— Why?

— Because that house has been empty for a very long time.

— The railway employee told me the same thing.

The woman looked surprised.

— You spoke to someone at the station?

— Yes.

— What did he tell you?

— He said the house had been empty for years.

The woman was silent again.

Emma became more curious.

— Is there something I should know about it?

The woman walked toward a shelf behind the counter. She reached for an old photograph and brought it back to the table.

— Look.

Emma took the photograph.

It showed a large house surrounded by trees. The building had two floors, tall windows, and a wide wooden porch. It looked almost exactly like the house Emma remembered from her childhood.

She looked more closely.

Several young people were standing in front of it.

Then she saw her grandmother.

Margaret.

She was perhaps twenty-two years old, smiling at the camera.

Emma's heart skipped.

— That's my grandmother.

The woman nodded.

— Her name is Mrs. Miller.

Emma looked at the photograph again.

There were six people in total.

Five stood together near the front steps, but one girl was slightly separated from the others. She had long dark hair and a serious expression.

Emma pointed to her.

— Who is she?

Mrs. Miller's eyes moved to the girl.

Her expression became uncomfortable.

— Eleanor.

— Eleanor who?

— Eleanor Hayes.

Emma waited.

— Was she a friend of my grandmother?

Mrs. Miller looked toward the café door.

— They were friends.

— What happened to her?

The woman took the photograph back.

— You should go.

Emma blinked.

— I'm sorry?

— Leave Blackwood before Halloween.

— My grandmother specifically told me to stay until Halloween.

Mrs. Miller lowered her voice.

— Then your grandmother made a terrible mistake.

Before Emma could respond, the café door opened.

An elderly man walked inside, leaning on a wooden walking stick. He wore a long brown coat and looked as though he had stepped out of another time.

He stopped when he saw Emma.

His eyes widened.

— Is that Margaret's granddaughter?

Emma turned toward him.

— Yes.

The man slowly approached.

— What's your name?

— Emma.

He studied her face.

— You look like her.

— Like my grandmother?

The old man nodded.

— Around the eyes.

He looked at Mrs. Miller.

— She came.

Mrs. Miller shook her head.

— Arthur, don't.

— She deserves to know.

— Not here.

Emma looked between them.

— Know what?

Arthur ignored the question.

— Did Margaret send you?

— Yes.

— Does she know what day it is?

Emma was confused.

— October 28.

Arthur's expression darkened.

— It has started early this year.

— What has started?

Mrs. Miller stepped forward.

— That's enough.

Arthur looked at Emma again.

— Listen to me carefully. If you're going to Willow Road, don't enter the house until you find the key.

Emma remembered the message from her grandmother.

The key is where it has always been.

— Where is the key?

Arthur looked at her for a long moment.

— You already know.

— I don't.

— Yes, you do.

He pointed toward the photograph.

Emma looked at it again.

The house.

Her grandmother.

The six young people.

Something about the image suddenly seemed familiar.

Then she remembered a garden from her childhood. She remembered her grandmother standing beside a stone angel near the front door.

— Under the angel — Emma whispered.

Arthur's expression changed.

Mrs. Miller closed her eyes.

— You remembered.

Emma looked at them.

— Remembered what?

A loud sound came from outside.

The church bell.

Everyone in the café went silent.

The first ring echoed through the square.

Then another.

Then another.

Emma counted without realizing it.

Four.

Five.

Six.

The bells continued.

Seven.

Eight.

Nine.

Ten.

Eleven.

Twelve.

Emma looked at the clock above the café counter.

It showed 7:00 p.m.

The thirteenth bell rang.

The lights went out.

Someone screamed outside.

For a few seconds, the entire café was swallowed by darkness.

Then the lights came back.

Mrs. Miller was standing beside the counter, her face completely pale.

Arthur looked at the door.

— Go.

Emma stared at him.

— What?

— Go to Willow Road. Now.

— Why?

— Because you must not be here when the bell rings again.

Emma looked through the window.

The fog had become much thicker.

She could barely see the other side of the square.

Then she heard a voice outside.

— Emma?

Her body went still.

She knew that voice.

Her grandmother.

— Emma, come home.

Emma moved toward the door.

Arthur grabbed her arm.

— Don't answer.

The voice came again.

— Emma, please.

She stared through the glass.

There was nobody outside.

Only fog.

She slowly pulled her arm free.

— That was my grandmother.

Arthur shook his head.

— No, it wasn't.

Emma picked up her suitcase.

Before leaving, she turned toward Mrs. Miller.

— Who was Eleanor?

The woman hesitated.

Arthur answered.

— A girl who disappeared on Halloween night.

Emma stared at him.

— When?

— 1956.

The number seemed to echo inside her head.

She looked at the photograph again.

Eleanor was smiling.

But there was something about her eyes that made Emma uncomfortable.

— What happened to her?

Arthur's expression became distant.

— Nobody knows.

He paused.

— At least, that's what we tell people.

Emma opened the café door.

Cold air rushed inside.

— What does that mean?

Arthur looked directly at her.

— It means some people in Blackwood remember what really happened.

Emma stepped outside.

The fog immediately surrounded her.

She turned back toward the café, but Arthur was already walking away.

Mrs. Miller stood behind the counter, watching her through the window.

Emma pulled her coat tighter and started walking toward Willow Road.

After a few minutes, she reached the edge of the square.

The street was almost empty now.

She looked ahead.

At the end of the road, barely visible through the fog, stood a large house.

Its windows were dark.

Except for one.

A single warm light glowed on the second floor.

Emma stopped.

The house was too far away to see clearly, but something about it felt familiar.

Then the light upstairs moved.

Not the light itself.

A shadow passed in front of the window.

Someone was standing there.

Watching her.

Emma's phone vibrated in her pocket.

She took it out.

For the first time since arriving in Blackwood, she had a signal.

One new message.

Emma stared at the screen.

The message had been sent from an unknown number.

DON'T GO TO THE HOUSE.

She looked toward the illuminated window.

The shadow was still there.

Then another message appeared.

HE IS WAITING FOR YOU.

chapters.title: The Road Through the Fog
chapters.content:
Emma stared at the message until the screen went dark.

For a moment, she considered turning around and going back to the café. Mrs. Miller had warned her. Arthur had warned her. Now someone who apparently knew exactly where she was had sent her the same warning.

But there was something else that bothered her even more.

He is waiting for you.

Who was he?

Emma looked at the house again. The shadow in the upstairs window had disappeared, but the light remained. It seemed impossible that anyone could be inside. The house looked as though it had been abandoned for decades.

She opened the message again and tried to reply.

Who are you?

The message failed to send.

No signal.

Emma stared at her phone in disbelief. The signal had disappeared as quickly as it had appeared.

She put the phone away and looked toward the road.

There was no one around.

The town behind her had become almost invisible beneath the fog. The last sounds from the market square were fading, and the cheerful Halloween decorations that had seemed so charming earlier now looked strangely out of place against the dark streets.

She thought of her grandmother.

Whatever was happening, Margaret had known about it. She had sent Emma here for a reason.

Emma took a deep breath and started walking.

The road to Willow Road was narrower than the main streets of Blackwood. Tall trees stood on both sides, their branches twisting overhead and blocking most of the remaining light from the sky. The fog moved slowly between their trunks, sometimes crossing the road in thick white clouds.

Emma pulled her suitcase behind her.

The wheels made a repetitive sound against the pavement.

Click.

Click.

Click.

She walked for several minutes without seeing another person.

Then she heard footsteps behind her.

Emma stopped.

The footsteps stopped too.

She looked over her shoulder.

There was nothing there.

Only the road disappearing into the fog.

She waited.

Nothing.

Emma started walking again.

A few seconds later, the footsteps returned.

This time they were closer.

She stopped once more.

The footsteps stopped.

Her heart began to beat faster.

— Is someone there?

No answer.

Emma looked around carefully. The trees were completely still now.

She continued walking, faster this time.

The footsteps followed.

She turned suddenly.

A dark figure stood in the middle of the road.

Emma froze.

It was a person, but the fog made it impossible to see their face. They were perhaps twenty meters away, standing perfectly still.

Emma's first thought was that it was the man from the house.

Her second was that she should run.

— Hello? — she called.

The figure didn't respond.

Instead, it slowly raised one arm and pointed down the road.

Emma looked in the direction it indicated.

Nothing.

When she turned back, the figure was gone.

She stared at the empty road.

— What is happening?

Her voice sounded small in the darkness.

Emma picked up her suitcase and hurried forward.

A few minutes later, she found a wooden sign.

WILLOW ROAD

She stopped beneath it.

At least she was going in the right direction.

She took out her phone.

7:21 p.m.

The walk from the town should have taken about fifteen minutes, but she had already been walking much longer than that.

She opened the map.

The blue dot showed her exactly where she expected to be.

Then the map moved.

The blue dot jumped backward.

Emma frowned.

She waited.

The dot moved again.

This time, it showed her several streets away, near the market square.

— That's impossible.

She refreshed the map.

The blue dot disappeared.

There was no signal again.

Emma put the phone away.

She continued down Willow Road.

The trees gradually gave way to old houses. Some had small gardens and wooden fences, while others appeared completely abandoned. Their windows were covered with boards, and weeds had grown through cracks in the sidewalks.

One house had a row of carved pumpkins along its front steps.

Every pumpkin had a candle inside.

Emma noticed that all the candles were burning.

She slowed down.

There was no one around.

The house appeared empty.

She kept walking.

Then something metallic struck the pavement behind her.

Emma turned.

Her suitcase was open.

She was certain she had closed it.

The zipper had moved almost all the way down, and several pieces of clothing had fallen onto the road.

— Seriously?

Emma put the suitcase down and began picking everything up.

As she lifted her sweater, she noticed something lying on top of the clothes.

A photograph.

She didn't recognize it at first.

Then she saw the house.

Her grandmother's house.

The same photograph she had seen in the café.

Emma picked it up and turned it over.

There was writing on the back.

The handwriting was unmistakably Margaret's.

Some doors should remain closed.

Emma stared at the sentence.

She had never seen the photograph before.

How had it gotten inside her suitcase?

She put it carefully into the front pocket and closed the suitcase again.

This time, she checked the zipper twice.

Then she continued.

The road seemed to become darker with every step.

At last, she saw the stone angel.

It stood beside a rusty iron gate, half-hidden beneath overgrown vines.

Emma stopped.

She remembered what Arthur had said.

Don't enter the house until you find the key.

She walked toward the statue.

The angel was old and badly damaged. One wing had broken away, and moss covered most of its face. Emma looked around the base.

Nothing.

She crouched down and moved the wet leaves aside.

Her fingers touched something hard.

She pulled it free.

A small metal box.

Emma wiped the dirt from its surface and opened it.

Inside was a large black key.

Beneath the key was another note.

She unfolded it.

Do not enter after midnight.

Emma looked at the time.

7:29 p.m.

She gave a nervous laugh.

— Well, at least I have plenty of time.

She put the note and key into her coat pocket.

Then she stood.

The gate was locked.

Emma inserted the key.

It fit perfectly.

She turned it.

Click.

The lock opened.

The gate swung inward with a long, rusty creak.

Beyond it, a narrow path disappeared into the fog.

And at the end of the path stood the house.

Emma had seen it in photographs, but nothing had prepared her for seeing it in person.

It was enormous.

Two stories rose above the overgrown garden, with tall windows and a wide wooden porch. The walls were dark with age, and ivy covered much of the eastern side. Several windows were broken, yet the front door looked strangely well maintained.

Emma stared at the second floor.

The light was still burning.

She felt the urge to turn around.

Instead, she stepped through the gate.

The moment her foot touched the path, the gate slammed shut behind her.

Emma spun around and grabbed the bars.

— No, no, no...

She pulled.

Nothing.

The lock had closed again.

Emma looked through the gate.

The road was still visible, but the fog was moving rapidly across it.

Within seconds, everything beyond the gate disappeared.

She was alone.

Emma turned back toward the house.

The upstairs light went out.

Her stomach tightened.

Then a second light came on.

Not upstairs.

In a small basement window.

Emma could see a figure standing behind the glass.

It was too far away to make out any details, but the person was clearly looking directly at her.

Emma took a step backward.

The figure slowly raised its hand.

It pointed toward the front door.

Emma looked.

The front door was opening.

Slowly.

No one was touching it.

The darkness inside the house seemed almost solid.

Emma stood frozen on the path.

Then a woman's voice came from the open doorway.

— Emma.

She knew that voice.

It was the voice from the café.

The voice that had sounded like her grandmother.

But now Emma understood something.

The woman in the darkness wasn't calling her grandmother's name.

She was calling hers.

— Emma...

The voice was softer this time.

Almost frightened.

Emma took one cautious step forward.

— Eleanor?

Silence.

Then, from somewhere inside the house, came a quiet answer.

— You came back.

chapters.title: A Light in the Window
chapters.content:
Emma stood motionless on the path, staring at the open doorway. The words echoed in her mind.

You came back.

She had never been to this house.

At least, she didn't remember ever being here.

The voice came again, softer than before.

— Emma...

She tightened her grip on the handle of her suitcase.

— Who are you?

There was no answer.

The basement window was dark now. Whoever had been standing behind it was gone.

Emma looked over her shoulder at the locked gate. The road beyond it had almost disappeared beneath the fog, but she could still see the faint outline of the stone angel.

She tried the gate once more.

It didn't move.

There was no way back.

She turned toward the house.

The open doorway seemed to be waiting for her.

Emma took a slow breath and walked up the steps.

The wooden porch creaked beneath her feet. She stopped at the entrance and looked inside.

The hall was completely dark.

She raised her phone and turned on the flashlight.

The beam revealed a large entrance hall with high ceilings and an old staircase directly ahead. Dust covered the floor, but strangely, there were no cobwebs around the doorway. The house looked abandoned, yet someone seemed to have taken care of certain parts of it.

Emma stepped inside.

The door closed behind her.

She turned immediately.

— Great.

She tried the handle.

Locked.

Emma pulled several times, but the door refused to open.

She took out the black key she had found beneath the stone angel and tried it in the lock.

Nothing.

She tried again.

Still nothing.

The key wasn't for this door.

Emma turned around and slowly examined the hallway.

Several paintings hung along the walls. Most showed unfamiliar people, but one caught her attention immediately.

It was a portrait of a young woman.

Emma moved closer.

The woman had long dark hair and pale skin. She wore a simple white dress and stood in front of the same house.

Emma recognized her from the photograph.

Eleanor.

She looked younger than she had appeared in the picture.

Emma studied the portrait.

There was something strange about the girl's expression. She wasn't smiling, but she didn't look sad either. She seemed to be staring directly at whoever stood in front of the painting.

Emma took a step closer.

The girl's eyes appeared to follow her.

She quickly looked away.

— It's just a painting.

She said it aloud because hearing her own voice made the house feel slightly less threatening.

Emma continued through the hallway.

At the end stood a grandfather clock.

Its wooden case was covered in dust, but the glass was surprisingly clean.

The clock had stopped at 7:30.

Emma checked her phone.

7:34.

She looked back at the clock.

The second hand moved.

Once.

Twice.

Three times.

Then the clock began ticking normally.

Emma stared.

The hands remained at 7:30.

She stepped away.

A faint sound came from upstairs.

Tap.

Tap.

Tap.

Someone was walking across the second floor.

Emma raised her phone toward the staircase.

— Hello?

The footsteps stopped.

She waited.

Nothing.

She considered leaving the house through a window, but the first floor windows were either locked or too small. She would have to find another exit.

Emma walked into the nearest room.

It was a dining room.

A long wooden table occupied the center, surrounded by twelve chairs. Dust covered the furniture, but the table itself looked strangely clean.

Emma moved closer.

There were twelve plates arranged around it.

Twelve glasses.

Twelve sets of silverware.

She frowned.

The house had supposedly been empty for decades.

Why would anyone have set the table?

Then she noticed something else.

One of the chairs was pulled away from the table.

A cup sat in front of it.

Steam rose from the surface.

Emma took a step backward.

The smell of tea filled the room.

Fresh tea.

She left immediately.

The next room was a living room.

An old fireplace occupied one wall, and above it hung a large photograph.

Emma raised her phone.

The photograph showed six young people standing in front of the house.

Her grandmother was there.

So was Eleanor.

Emma recognized the others from the photograph she had seen at the café.

But now she noticed something she hadn't seen before.

A seventh figure stood behind them.

A young man.

His face was turned away from the camera.

Emma moved closer.

She couldn't see his features.

She looked at the photograph from the café in her memory.

There had only been six people.

Why was this one different?

Emma touched the photograph.

The glass was cold.

Then she heard a voice behind her.

— Don't.

Emma turned.

The room was empty.

She stepped backward.

— Eleanor?

No answer.

The voice had sounded very close.

Emma looked at the fireplace.

Something had been carved into the wood above it.

A circle.

Inside the circle was the number thirteen.

She touched it.

Nothing happened.

Then she heard a faint click.

Emma jumped.

One of the bookshelves moved slightly.

She approached it.

Behind the bookshelf was a narrow gap.

Emma pushed.

The shelf moved another few centimeters.

There was a hidden passage behind it.

She stared into the darkness.

A cold draft came from inside.

Emma's first instinct was to leave it alone.

Her second was to investigate.

She reached for her phone.

The screen suddenly went black.

The battery was completely dead.

— You have got to be kidding me.

Emma pressed the power button several times.

Nothing.

She looked toward the hallway.

The house was silent.

Then she heard a sound upstairs.

A door opening.

Emma raised her head.

A shadow appeared at the top of the staircase.

Someone was standing there.

Emma couldn't see their face.

The figure remained still for several seconds.

Then it slowly walked toward the stairs.

Emma stepped backward.

The figure took the first step down.

Then the second.

Emma turned and ran.

She rushed into the dining room and crouched behind one of the chairs.

Her breathing was loud.

She covered her mouth.

The footsteps continued.

Slow.

Heavy.

The figure reached the bottom of the stairs.

Emma watched from behind the chair.

A man walked into the hallway.

He was tall and thin, wearing a black suit that seemed strangely old-fashioned.

His face remained hidden in shadow.

He stopped near the living room.

Emma held her breath.

The man turned his head.

For one terrible moment, Emma thought he had seen her.

But he simply walked toward the front door.

He stood there.

Waiting.

Then he spoke.

— You shouldn't have come tonight.

Emma didn't move.

The man remained facing the door.

— She told you to come, didn't she?

Emma's heart raced.

He knew about her grandmother.

The man slowly turned around.

Emma could finally see his face.

Dark hair.

Pale skin.

Sharp eyes.

And a small scar above his eyebrow.

She had seen him before.

In the photograph.

The seventh figure.

The man smiled.

— Margaret always was very good at keeping secrets.

Emma stood up.

— Who are you?

His smile disappeared.

— You don't remember me?

Emma stared at him.

There was something familiar about his face, but she couldn't understand why.

— No.

The man took one step toward her.

— That's unfortunate.

Another step.

— Because I remember you.

Emma backed away.

— How could you remember me? I've never been here.

The man's expression became strangely sad.

— Not in this life.

Emma's blood ran cold.

He turned toward the staircase.

— You need to leave before midnight.

Emma glanced at the front door.

— Then open it.

The man looked back at her.

— I can't.

— Why not?

He pointed toward the grandfather clock.

The hands had begun moving.

7:30.

7:31.

7:32.

Emma stared.

— What time is it really?

The man didn't answer.

The clock continued ticking.

7:33.

7:34.

Then suddenly—

7:35.

Every light in the house went out.

The man disappeared.

Emma stood alone in the darkness.

A whisper came from behind her.

— Don't trust him.

Emma turned.

A pale figure stood at the entrance to the living room.

Long dark hair.

White dress.

Bare feet.

Eleanor.

Emma stared at her.

— Are you real?

Eleanor didn't answer.

She raised one hand and pointed toward the staircase.

— Your grandmother hid something upstairs.

Emma looked at the stairs.

— What?

Eleanor's expression became frightened.

— Something he must never find.

Then she looked behind Emma.

Her face changed completely.

Fear.

— He's coming back.

The grandfather clock suddenly struck.

Once.

Emma looked at it.

7:36.

The clock struck again.

Twice.

Then a third time.

Eleanor whispered:

— You have to find it before he does.

The fourth strike echoed through the house.

And somewhere upstairs, a door slammed shut.

chapters.title: The Locked Gate
chapters.content:
Emma remained at the bottom of the staircase, listening to the echo of the door upstairs. Eleanor had disappeared again, leaving behind only the faint scent of something floral in the cold air. Emma wanted to believe that she had imagined the girl, that exhaustion and fear had somehow turned old photographs and shadows into something that looked alive. But the locked house, the moving clock, and the man who claimed to remember her made that explanation increasingly difficult to accept.

She looked toward the front door. The man was gone, but the door remained closed.

Emma crossed the hallway and tried the handle again. It didn't move. She pulled harder, then pressed her shoulder against the wood. Nothing.

— Open the door!

Her voice echoed through the empty house.

No one answered.

Emma stepped back and looked at the lock. The black key from beneath the stone angel was still in her pocket. She took it out and tried it, although she already knew it wouldn't work.

The key turned halfway and stopped.

Emma frowned.

She tried again.

Nothing.

She was about to remove it when she heard a faint click from somewhere inside the door.

The lock had moved.

Emma pulled the handle.

The door opened.

She nearly stumbled forward.

Cold fog rolled across the porch and into the hallway. Emma stepped outside, expecting to see the path and the gate, but the garden looked completely different.

The fog was so thick that she could barely see her hands.

She walked down the steps and searched for the gate.

It wasn't there.

Emma turned around.

The house was still behind her, but it looked farther away than it had moments before.

— This isn't possible.

She walked forward, hoping the gate would appear through the fog.

Instead, she found herself standing beside the stone angel.

The statue was covered with moisture, and its broken wing seemed almost black in the darkness. Emma looked around its base.

She remembered the moment she had found the key.

Under the angel.

She crouched and brushed the wet leaves away.

There was a small metal box.

Emma stared at it.

She had already found the key there.

So why was the box here again?

She opened it.

Inside was another key.

This one was silver.

Underneath it lay a folded piece of paper.

Emma opened the note.

The handwriting was her grandmother's.

If you find this key, you have already opened the wrong door.

Emma read the sentence twice.

Then she looked at the house.

One of the upstairs windows was illuminated.

A figure stood behind the glass.

Emma couldn't see the face, but she knew who it was.

The man.

He raised his hand.

Emma stepped backward.

The figure disappeared.

She looked down at the silver key.

There was a number engraved on it.

13.

The fog moved around her feet.

Emma stood and looked toward the gate.

This time, she could see it.

It was only a few meters away.

She ran toward it.

The iron gate opened easily when she touched it.

Emma stepped through and immediately turned around.

The house was still there.

The garden was still there.

Everything looked normal.

For the first time since entering the house, Emma could see the road beyond the gate.

She took a deep breath.

Then she heard footsteps behind her.

Emma turned.

The road was empty.

She hurried away from the house.

She didn't stop until she reached the main road.

The fog was thinner here, and several streetlights were visible in the distance.

Emma checked her phone.

9:02 p.m.

She stared at the screen.

She had been inside the house for less than two hours, but it felt like an entire night had passed.

The phone suddenly vibrated.

A message appeared.

UNKNOWN NUMBER

Where are you?

Emma typed:

Who is this?

The message sent.

A reply appeared almost immediately.

Someone who is trying to keep you alive.

Emma stopped walking.

How do you know where I am?

There was no answer.

She waited.

Then another message appeared.

Go to the market square. Find the old woman with the gray coat.

Emma looked around.

The streets were empty.

She turned toward the market.

As she walked, the fog began to lift.

The familiar buildings appeared again.

The bakery.

The bookstore.

The café.

Emma pushed open the café door.

The brass bell rang.

Mrs. Miller was still there.

She looked up.

Her eyes widened.

— You came back.

Emma closed the door behind her.

— I need to talk to you.

Mrs. Miller looked at Emma's coat, then at the silver key in her hand.

Her face became pale.

— Where did you get that?

— Under the stone angel.

Mrs. Miller stared at the key.

— You weren't supposed to find it yet.

— What is it?

The woman looked toward the windows.

— Not here.

Emma approached the counter.

— Then tell me somewhere else.

Mrs. Miller hesitated.

Finally, she locked the café door.

— Sit down.

Emma sat.

Mrs. Miller pulled a chair across from her.

For several seconds, she said nothing.

Then she asked:

— Did you see him?

Emma knew immediately who she meant.

— The man in the house?

Mrs. Miller nodded.

— Yes.

— Did he tell you his name?

— No.

— Did he say he remembered you?

Emma's expression changed.

— Yes.

Mrs. Miller closed her eyes.

— Then it has begun.

Emma leaned forward.

— What has begun?

Mrs. Miller looked at her.

— The same thing that happened in 1956.

— Eleanor's disappearance?

— No.

She lowered her voice.

— Everything that happened before it.

Emma felt a chill.

— I don't understand.

Mrs. Miller stood and walked toward the photograph she had shown Emma earlier.

She took it from the shelf and placed it on the table.

— This photograph was taken on October 28, 1956.

Emma looked at the six young people.

— Three days before Eleanor disappeared.

— Yes.

Mrs. Miller pointed to Margaret.

— Your grandmother was one of them.

Then she pointed to Eleanor.

— She was another.

Finally, she pointed to the young man Emma had seen in the house.

— And he was the seventh.

Emma looked at her.

— You said there were six people.

— There were.

Emma's eyes narrowed.

— Then who is he?

Mrs. Miller looked at the photograph.

— His name was Thomas Carter.

Emma's stomach tightened.

— Carter?

— Yes.

— Was he related to my grandmother?

Mrs. Miller didn't answer.

That was enough.

Emma looked at the photograph again.

— Who was he?

Mrs. Miller took a slow breath.

— Margaret's older brother.

Emma felt suddenly cold.

— My great-uncle?

— Yes.

— But the newspaper said Thomas Hayes.

Mrs. Miller looked surprised.

— You read the newspaper?

— I found it in the house.

The old woman became visibly nervous.

— You shouldn't have found that.

— Why?

Mrs. Miller leaned closer.

— Because the newspaper was written to hide the truth.

Emma stared at her.

— What truth?

Before Mrs. Miller could answer, something struck the café window.

Bang.

Emma jumped.

Both women turned.

Nothing was outside.

Then another sound.

Bang.

This time from the back door.

Mrs. Miller stood.

— Stay here.

She walked toward the kitchen.

Emma followed.

— What is it?

Mrs. Miller didn't answer.

The back door began to shake.

Someone was knocking.

Three times.

Slowly.

Knock.

Knock.

Knock.

Mrs. Miller's face lost all color.

— Don't open it.

Emma stared at the door.

A voice came from the other side.

— Margaret?

Mrs. Miller stepped backward.

The voice came again.

— Margaret, it's me.

Emma recognized it.

It was the man from the house.

Thomas.

Mrs. Miller whispered:

— He shouldn't be able to leave the house.

The door handle began to turn.

Emma looked at the silver key in her hand.

The number thirteen seemed to catch the light.

Then she heard another voice.

This one came from behind her.

— He's lying.

Emma turned.

Eleanor stood at the end of the kitchen.

Her white dress was covered with dirt, and her dark hair hung over one side of her face.

She looked directly at Emma.

— Thomas isn't the one you should be afraid of.

Emma stared at her.

— Then who should I be afraid of?

Eleanor looked toward the locked door.

Her voice became barely audible.

— Your grandmother.
